payload.title: What Are the Lebanese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s, often Lebanese-Australian or with one Lebanese-heritage partner (Maronite or other Christian, Sunni or Shia Muslim, or Druze family), planning a luxury wedding outside Lebanon who want to know what each custom means, from the formal asking and henna night to the zaffeh, dabke and sword-cut cake, and how to carry them into a celebration in Italy, Cyprus, the UAE or Australia.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the section on bringing Lebanese customs to a wedding elsewhere.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the 'bringing the customs abroad' section)
payload.angle: Page-one listicles, and our own old page (slugged 7, titled 12), list fireworks, a 'no grand exit' and multi-day parties as universal, make unsourced legal claims and invite couples to marry 'from Beirut to Lake Como'. Smartraveller rates Lebanon 'Do not travel' (updated 24 September 2026, still current 3 November 2026) and warns that celebratory gunfire at weddings has caused casualties. So we write for Lebanese-Australian and mixed-heritage couples bringing these customs to weddings elsewhere: a Lebanese wedding in order, before the day (the formal asking, engagement, henna night, leaving the family home, church crowning or katb al-kitab) and the celebration (zaffeh, dabke, zaghareet, sword and cake, sugared almonds and sweets), each meaning sourced or labelled 'often told', a clear note that customs differ between Christian, Muslim and Druze families, practical notes on staging each one abroad, and a short, honest travel and legal note (no suggestion to marry in Lebanon).
must_include: Exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways at the top.

11 customs (12 if UNESCO links Al-Zajal to weddings) from tradition_plan in wedding order, grouped 'Before the wedding' (batch A) and 'The celebration' (batch B), each with a sourced meaning; unsourced origins labelled 'often told' (no [[VERIFY]] marker) or left out. Arabic terms transliterated consistently (tulbeh, khutbeh, laylat al-henna, zaffeh, dabke, zaghareet (singular zaghrouta), katb al-kitab, mlabbas), with the first spelling variant given once.

One early line that Lebanese weddings span Maronite and other Christian, Sunni and Shia Muslim and Druze families, so customs vary by faith, region and family; never present every custom as religious or universal; faith or regional notes only where sourced. Culture, not politics.

A section on bringing the customs to a wedding elsewhere (Italy, Cyprus, the UAE, Australia): what each custom needs on the day (space for a zaffeh procession and dabke line, timing for a henna night, a ceremonial blade and venue rules for the cake). Link the two Lebanese Real Weddings in Italy. No vendor or venue names, no prices.

Short travel and legal note, 'as at November 2026': Smartraveller overall 'Do not travel' to Lebanon (updated 24 September 2026, still current 3 November 2026); Smartraveller says family law, including marriage, is based on local religious laws; state 'civil marriage is not performed in Lebanon' ONLY if an official source says so, otherwise omit; Lebanese dual nationals are treated as Lebanese citizens; 'check with the Australian Embassy in Beirut and Smartraveller before any travel'; no implied help with legal paperwork; recognition in Australia via the register-at-home link only.

Internal links: pillar /expert-advice/wedding-traditions in intro and close; /a-traditional-lebanese-destination-wedding-in-lake-como-italy and /a-lebanese-medieval-destination-wedding-in-italy from the abroad section; /destinations/middle-east; /expert-advice/palestinian-wedding-traditions only at zaffeh or dabke where the shared custom is sourced.

Short FAQ (5 to 6 questions) from SEO People Also Ask, sourced answers only; primary CTA /magazine, secondary Wedded Advisor CTA after the abroad section; Advisor claims only from brand-facts.md (single point of contact; fee and inclusions agreed in writing), never 'from first idea to the last dance'.

tradition_plan.note: Planner fact-checks in 2 parallel batches with separate scratch folders (02-research/batch-a, 02-research/batch-b), 15 min HARD, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds. Preferred sources: UNESCO ICH (ich.unesco.org), Lebanese Ministry of Tourism or Ministry of Culture pages, Maronite Patriarchate or Antiochian Orthodox liturgical texts, museums, Britannica or Encyclopaedia of Islam, academic sources (ethnomusicology for zaffeh, dabke, zaghareet). Never competitor wedding sites or blogs as sole source. Smartraveller already fetched (02-research/pages/smartraveller.md); do not re-fetch. Old page notes in 02-research/pages/old-lebanese.md.
tradition_plan.count: 11 customs plus the travel and legal note (6 in batch A; 5 customs, Al-Zajal if UNESCO-linked, plus the note in batch B)

batch_A.tradition: The formal asking (tulbeh or toulbe): the groom's family visits the bride's family to ask for her hand
facts_to_source: What the tulbeh is and who attends (groom with parents and elders) from an encyclopaedic, academic or Lebanese official source; coffee served at the visit only if sourced, otherwise 'often told'
Spelling variants as a source prints them
Any faith differences only if sourced
Engagement as a formal family stage, and ring exchange, from an academic or encyclopaedic source
Scale of the engagement party: no 'rivals the wedding' claim unless sourced; 'often told' otherwise
No claims about who pays
Henna night as a pre-wedding gathering in Lebanon and the Levant from an academic or museum source; which communities hold it (some Muslim and some Christian families) only if sourced
What happens (henna applied to the bride's hands, women of both families, songs) from a source; otherwise 'often told'
Drop old details: red roses from the groom, bride in gown, gold or diamonds from the groom's parents, unless sourced

batch_A.tradition: The bride's departure from the family home (the groom's party collects her, often with a zaffeh at her door)
facts_to_source: The groom and his family collecting the bride from her parents' home from an academic or encyclopaedic source
Songs or zaghareet at the departure only if sourced
Keep emotional framing respectful; no 'giving away' claims unless sourced

batch_A.tradition: The church ceremony and the crowning (Maronite and Orthodox weddings)
facts_to_source: Crowning in the Maronite and Antiochian Orthodox rites from a church or liturgical source (Maronite Patriarchate, Antiochian Orthodox archdiocese, Britannica or academic)
What the crowns symbolise only as the source states (drop old 'king and queen', candlelight and 'same weight as rings' unless sourced)
Whether koumbaros or sponsors hold the crowns only if sourced for Lebanon

batch_A.tradition: Katb al-kitab: signing the marriage contract (Muslim families; Druze practice only if sourced)
facts_to_source: What katb al-kitab is (marriage contract signed before a sheikh or religious official with witnesses) from Encyclopaedia of Islam, Britannica or academic source
Mahr (dower) named only as the source defines it; no amounts
Timing (separate from or on the day of the reception) only if sourced; Druze marriage contract only from a sourced text; Sunni and Shia differences only if sourced

batch_B.tradition: The zaffeh: drum and dance procession
facts_to_source: Zaffeh definition (procession with drums, dancers and singers, often with swords or torches) from an ethnomusicology, encyclopaedic or official tourism source
Shared Levantine custom (link the Palestinian draft) only if a source makes the link
Drop 'most requested moment' and 'the best troupes travel' claims
Dabke as a Levantine folk line dance, the leader (raas or lawweeh) and handkerchief, from an ethnomusicology or encyclopaedic source
UNESCO: cite only a listing whose page names Lebanon; do not cite a listing for another state as Lebanese
Instruments (derbakeh or tabl, mijwiz) only if sourced
Definition of zaghrouta (plural zaghareet), also zalghouta in Lebanese usage, from a dictionary, encyclopaedic or ethnomusicology source
Accompanying sung verses (ahazij) only if sourced
Used across Levantine and wider Arab weddings: one line, sourced
Cutting the cake with a sword at Lebanese weddings: source from an academic, museum or official tourism text; otherwise 'often told' with no origin story
No 'family heirloom' or 'ceremonial blade' generalisation unless sourced
Practical note for abroad: venue rules on blades are 'check with the venue' (no [[VERIFY]] needed)
Sugared almonds as wedding favours in Lebanon and their meaning (odd numbers, wishes) only if sourced; otherwise 'often told'
Sweets served (baklava, ma'amoul, knafeh) named without claims of tradition unless sourced
No prices or supplier names
Include ONLY if the UNESCO ICH page for Al-Zajal (Lebanon, 2014) is live, names Lebanon and links it to weddings or family celebrations; quote the year and wording from the page
If not linked to weddings, drop it entirely and do not mention UNESCO

batch_B.tradition: Travel and legal note (not a custom)
facts_to_source: Smartraveller level, dates and Embassy: already in 02-research/pages/smartraveller.md (do not re-fetch)

'Civil marriage is not performed in Lebanon': only from an official source (Lebanese government, DFAT or Australian Embassy Beirut); otherwise omit and say family law is based on religious law (Smartraveller)
Registering an overseas marriage at home: link our existing guide, no new legal claims
